sections.heading: The Legacy Problem and Its Limits
sections.md:
## The Legacy Problem and Its Limits

The board review examined the current Vega1 stack in full: 31 distinct problems spread across 8 categories. Alongside that inventory, the review placed four architecture proposals side by side — Arc-A, Arc-B, Arc-C, and a re-cut version, Arc-T — setting up the comparison that the rest of this deck works through.

The central question the review had to settle first: can the legacy system simply be patched instead of rebuilt? The answer is that patching is a delay, not a fix. Applying fixes to the existing Vega1 stack buys roughly 2-3 years of runway. But that runway runs out on a fixed clock — the underlying hardware is running end-of-life Windows, and by 2031-2032 a rebuild becomes unavoidable. At that point it happens under deadline pressure, on infrastructure that is already past its supported life, which is a materially worse position than choosing the timing now.

The gap patching leaves in place is visible in concrete scenarios, not just architecture diagrams. Take the Belvedere welcome scenario: today's legacy system delivers about 10% of the intended experience. Arc-T, by contrast, is designed to deliver 100% of that same scenario. That is not a marginal improvement — it is the difference between a system that structurally cannot support the intended customer experience and one built to support it from the ground up.

Taken together, these findings frame the rest of the deck: the legacy system's problems are broad (29 issues, 8 categories), patching them only rents time before an end-of-life-hardware deadline forces the issue anyway, and the experience cost of staying on legacy is already measurable today, not hypothetical.

sections.heading: Four Architectures, One Scorecard
sections.md:
## Four Architectures, One Scorecard

Four rebuild paths were put through the same scorecard — timeline to ship, risk profile, how many of the 29 known legacy problems each closes, how many of 11 unexamined principles each closes, and how many single points of failure (SPOFs) remain. The four are:

- **Arc-A** — Event-sourced spine (Postgres + NATS + .NET)
- **Arc-B** — Reactive actor mesh (Rust + iroh)
- **Arc-C** — SQLite-as-the-system, MCP-first (Bun)
- **Arc-T** — Six layers: Substrate / Signal / Ontology / Intent+Safety / Surface / Federation

### Timeline, risk, and closure

| Architecture | Agentic v1 | Agentic v2 | Risk | Problems closed (of 31) | Principles closed (of 11) | SPOF count |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Arc-A | 8-10 wk | 24 wk | Low | 26 | 0 | 1 (Postgres) |
| Arc-B | 12-16 wk | 36 wk | Medium | 24 | 0 | 0 |
| Arc-C | 5-7 wk | 20 wk | Medium | 25 | 0 | 1 (SQLite) |
| Arc-T | 14-20 wk | 48 wk | Medium-high | 29 | 11 | 0 |

Arc-A closes 26 of the 31 legacy problems, Arc-B closes 24, and Arc-C closes 25. Arc-T is the only option that closes all 31. On the 11 unexamined principles — risks nobody has mapped yet — Arc-A, Arc-B, and Arc-C close none of them, while Arc-T closes all 11. This is the core trade-off: Arc-T is the slowest to ship (14-20 weeks for v1, 48 weeks for v2, versus as little as 5-7 weeks for Arc-C) and carries the highest risk rating, but it is the only architecture that closes everything — every known problem and every unexamined principle.

### Single points of failure

SPOF counts diverge sharply: Arc-A has 1 (Postgres), Arc-B has 0, Arc-C has 1 (SQLite), and Arc-T has 0. Fewer SPOFs means fewer ways the whole system can go down at once — Arc-B and Arc-T eliminate this risk entirely, while Arc-A and Arc-C each still depend on a single database layer.

### Decision matrix: speed and hiring vs. future-proofing

A second cut of the data — restricted to Arc-A, Arc-C, and Arc-T — scores three criteria: time to first customer install (high weight), future-proofing for 2030 KNX-IoT + Matter + AI (high weight), and whether the team can ship without hiring (medium weight).

| Criterion | Arc-A | Arc-C | Arc-T |
|---|---|---|---|
| Time to first customer install | 8-10 wk | 5-7 wk | 14-20 wk |
| Future-proof for 2030 (KNX-IoT + Matter + AI) | medium | medium | high |
| Ship without hiring | yes (.NET) | yes (TS) | no (needs a Quint formal-methods contractor plus Rust ramp-up) |

Arc-A and Arc-C both beat Arc-T on time-to-first-install and can ship with the existing team's current stack (.NET or TypeScript) with no new hires. Arc-T alone scores high on future-proofing for 2030-era smart-home standards and AI integration, but it requires bringing in a Quint formal-methods contractor and ramping the team on Rust. This is why the fast, hiring-free options and the future-proof option cannot both win: speed and internal-only staffing pull one way, long-term durability pulls the other.

sections.heading: Arc-T's Complete Fix
sections.md:
Among the four architectures scored against the legacy system, only Arc-T re-cuts the underlying layers rather than working within the existing mental model. Rulings across the evaluation confirm Arc-T closes all 31 legacy problems identified during the audit, and clears all 11 principles that had gone unexamined under the legacy design. The other three proposals were scored differently: each retains the legacy mental model, meaning they patch symptoms inside the same layer boundaries rather than restructuring them. That distinction is why Arc-T stands apart — it is the only option that actually fixes everything the audit surfaced, not a subset of it.

Part of what makes this closure credible is the rigor behind Arc-T's safety design. Alex's safety frame — the component governing behavior at the architecture's lowest layer — defines 15 distinct invariants. These invariants are enforced by the L3 safety kernel, meaning safety guarantees are not aspirational or process-based but built into the layer that sits beneath everything else Arc-T does. The invariant count is a concrete engineering artifact: each invariant is a rule the kernel actively enforces, not a guideline teams are asked to follow.

Together, the two facts reinforce each other. Arc-T's claim to closing 29/31 problems and 11/11 principles is not just a scoring outcome — it is backed by an enforcement mechanism (the 15-invariant safety kernel) that gives the "closes everything" verdict a mechanical guarantee rather than a design intention. Where the other three proposals leave enforcement implicit within the legacy model, Arc-T makes it explicit and load-bearing at the lowest layer of the stack.

sections.heading: The Phased Rebuild Recommendation
sections.md:
## The Recommendation

The proposal is to invest in a rebuild rather than continue patching the legacy system. The path is phased in two stages:

- **Arc-A** — a 6-month MVP doorway. Ships fast, proves the architecture, gets a working system into production sooner.
- **Arc-T** — a 12-month long-bet. The fuller architecture that closes the remaining gaps the MVP doesn't address.

### Why the phasing isn't a compromise

A natural worry with any "start small" plan is that the small version becomes throwaway work if the team later decides to go bigger. That isn't the case here: Arc-A's event log becomes Arc-T's substrate history later. The data and history the MVP generates carries forward directly into the long-bet architecture, so choosing the safer, faster MVP path does not forfeit the option to build the fuller system afterward. Every week Arc-A runs in production is a week of substrate history Arc-T inherits for free.

### The cost of going further

Pursuing Arc-T is not free of new spend beyond engineering time: it requires budget for one Quint formal-methods contractor, engaged for 6 weeks. This is the one concrete extra line item tied to the future-proof option, used to formally verify the harder guarantees Arc-T is meant to deliver.

### The framing

The recommendation closes on a deliberately stark line: pay agent-weeks now, or pay architect-years later. That is the choice being put in front of the decision-makers — a modest, bounded spend today (the MVP build plus a 6-week specialist engagement) against a much larger, less bounded cost if the rebuild is deferred and the legacy system's problems compound instead.

sections.heading: The Board's Decision
sections.md:
The board's task today is deliberately narrow: one binary decision, cleanly separated from the open questions that follow it.

The headline vote is patch versus rebuild. If the board chooses to patch, the discussion ends there — legacy continues with incremental fixes. If the board chooses to rebuild, a second-order choice follows immediately: which architecture lane to commit to. The framing offers two named options — Arc-A, positioned as the safe choice, and Arc-T, positioned as the future-proof choice. This is presented as the exact decision the board needs to make today, with no additional scope folded into it.

Beyond this headline vote, seven further questions remain open and are explicitly flagged as unresolved rather than decided in this session:

- Patch or rebuild, restated as the binary itself.
- If rebuild is chosen, which lane — Arc-A, Arc-T, or Arc-C.
- The multi-tenant horizon the solution should target: a near-term scale of one to ten buildings, or a much larger scale of one hundred to one thousand.
- Whether AI should be treated as a load-bearing differentiator for the product, a yes/no strategic call.
- Whether federation across homes should be built into version 1, or deferred to version 2.
- Whether budget will be allocated for one Quint formal-methods contractor over a six-week engagement — a question that applies specifically to the Arc-T lane.
- Which site serves as the pilot for version 1, with Marco, Belvedere, and Alex named as the candidate options.

Together, this closes the topic — and the deck — by isolating the single decision that must be made now (patch vs. rebuild, and if rebuild, Arc-A vs. Arc-T) from the broader set of strategic and logistical questions that still need answers afterward.
